summary: For ages 5–7: rainforests hold an enormous variety of plants — towering kapok and Brazil nut trees, climbing vines called lianas, colourful orchids (many of which grow high on tree branches rather than in the ground), giant water lilies big enough to hold a small child, and huge pointed leaves that funnel rainwater off their tips. The core goal is recognising this variety and giant scale with vivid hooks, plus seeding the surprising idea that some plants grow high up and have clever shapes for a wet, crowded, shady world (adaptations are developed fully in a later 7–9 topic).
misconceptions: All rainforest plants are ordinary and small — many are giants or grow in surprising ways
Flowers only grow in the ground — orchids grow high up on tree branches
Vines are separate stringy things — lianas are climbing plants using trees to reach the light
Big leaves are just decoration — their shape helps shed heavy rain
Plants are the same everywhere — rainforests have an extraordinary variety of plant forms

activities.title: Rainforest plant gallery: variety and giant scale
steps: Look at real photographs of a kapok tree, Brazil nut tree, liana, orchid, giant water lily, and a drip-tip leaf.
For the kapok, compare it to a scale reference such as a child-sized figure or a house to feel 'taller than a house'.
For the liana, trace how the rope-like vine spirals up a trunk toward the light.
For the orchid, look at a branch close-up showing the flower growing ON the tree, not in soil.
For the giant water lily, see a pad big enough to hold a small child floating on water.
For the drip-tip leaf, watch or imagine a stream of rain tipping neatly off the pointed tip.
Give each plant a one-line hook and say it aloud: kapok = giant tree; liana = climbing rope; orchid = flower that lives on a branch; giant lily = big enough to sit a child; drip-leaf = funnels rain.
Name at least two rainforest plants, then describe one of them (a giant tree, a climbing vine, or a flower on a branch).
activities.insight: Rainforest plants aren't all ordinary and small — they come in an extraordinary variety, many are giants, and some grow in surprising places and shapes for a wet, crowded, shady forest.

activities.title: Why such strange shapes? A hook for clever forms
steps: Act out or pour water onto a large pointed leaf (a real leaf, or a laminated or waxed card stand-in that only approximates the real leaf — plain paper soaks up water and may not shed it) and watch it run off the tip; describe where the rain goes.
Pretend to be a liana: start low in the 'shade' and climb (with hands or a rope) up toward a 'light' at the top of the forest.
Open a lift-the-flap or answer the question 'Why such strange shapes?' and talk about the wet, crowded, shady forest.
Point to one plant and say one clever thing about its shape (a vine that climbs to reach light, a leaf that funnels rain).
activities.insight: Some rainforest plants have clever shapes and habits — climbing to reach light, funnelling off heavy rain — that help them thrive in a giant green world. This seeds the later idea of plant adaptations.

activities.title: Check and discuss: the orchid on the branch
steps: Respond to: 'An orchid grows high up on the branch of a big rainforest tree, not in the ground. Is the orchid stealing food from the tree like a thief? Say yes or no, and then say WHY it grows up there.'
Match each plant to a feature (giant tree, climbing vine, flower on a branch, rain-funnelling leaf) after browsing the gallery.

Discuss follow-ups: Where does a plant get its food — the soil, or something else? Why would it be hard for a small plant to live on the dark forest floor? What is a liana, and how does it reach the top of the forest?
activities.insight: A perching orchid isn't a thief: it grows high only to reach sunlight and makes its own food from sunlight, taking water from air and rain — not from the tree. Tall and climbing growth is about competing for light above the shady floor.

checkQuestion: An orchid grows high up on the branch of a big rainforest tree, not in the ground. Is the orchid stealing food from the tree like a thief? Tell me yes or no, and then tell me WHY it grows up there.
checkAnswer: No — the orchid isn't stealing from the tree. It just perches on the branch to get up high near the sunlight, because plants on the dark floor can't get enough light. It makes its own food from sunlight and takes water from the air and rain, not from the tree. Climbing up is how it reaches the light.
